title: The kirpan, explained
hook: the word is often explained as kirpa and aan, mercy and honor

segments.voice: Yesterday, two flags at the Akal Takht, and your line, spirit a little higher. Today, the small sword every initiated Sikh wears, and what its name is said to hold. Day two hundred seventy-six.

Airports, schools, courtrooms. Again and again, the kirpan has made headlines when a security guard spots it: a small curved blade in a sheath, worn on a cloth strap under a Sikh's clothes. The headlines usually ask one question. Is it a weapon? A few days ago we met the kirpan as one of the five Ks. Today we slow down on something the headlines skip. Before anyone argues about what it is, listen to what its name is often said to mean. Today: the kirpan, explained.
screen: `AIRPORTS, SCHOOLS, COURTROOMS.` → `IS IT A WEAPON?` → `FIRST, LISTEN TO THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Sikh teachers often explain the word kirpan by splitting it in two. Kirpa: grace, mercy, kindness. The same word appears in the Guru Granth Sahib again and again for God's grace, the gift nobody earns. And aan: honor, dignity, self-respect. Kirpa plus aan. Mercy and honor. Here's the honest part. Language scholars trace kirpan to an older Sanskrit word, kripana, which simply means a sword or a knife. So the mercy-and-honor reading is best understood as a teaching explanation, the way a teacher might unpack a word, rather than its original root. But notice which part comes first in the explanation. Kirpa. Mercy leads. Honor follows. The kirpan is worn as a reminder of a duty: to protect the weak, to stand for justice, to guard the dignity of others as well as your own. It's never meant for anger or for show. The Sikh code of conduct lists it among the five Ks an initiated Sikh keeps on at all times. Sikhs often wear a small one, some only a few inches long, and they will tell you that the moment it's drawn in temper, its meaning is lost. So the kirpan carries its own warning. A blade that is mostly mercy. That's why, where courts have looked closely, some have accepted it as a religious article, with safeguards, rather than a weapon. And that's why Sikhs say its real work happens in the sheath. It's a reminder that you're responsible for the people around you, and that mercy comes first.
screen: `KIRPA — GRACE, MERCY.` · `AAN — HONOR, DIGNITY.` · `THE ROOT: SANSKRIT KRIPANA, A BLADE.` · `MERCY LEADS, HONOR FOLLOWS.` · then, large: `MERCY FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you're a little annoyed with right now. Someone who owes you an apology, or who got something wrong. Picture them clearly. Now, instead of rehearsing what you'd say, ask what mercy would look like here. Not pretending it didn't matter: that would cost your honor. Just a little grace, offered first. Maybe a softer message, maybe letting one thing go. Choose one merciful act you could do today. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The kirpan. The small sword of an initiated Sikh, often explained as kirpa and aan, mercy and honor. Mercy comes first.
Your line: mercy first. Today, do the merciful thing you chose, before you decide whether you were right. Day two hundred seventy-six.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kirpan, the small sword; often explained as kirpa (mercy) + aan (honor).

what a scholar hears: the word descends from Sanskrit kripana, a sword or knife; kirpa-plus-aan is a homiletic reading, and some courts have accepted the kirpan as a religious article with safeguards.
